doc.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Holons, Bach as consolidator and Ellington's whole history of jazz
summary: Transcend and include: Bach consolidated, and Ellington's band carried all jazz history.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: same thing. And in one of those books, I think it was the one on science, he was one of the first people to start using this term “holon” H-O-L-O-N which is the concept of how the universe is really put together, because since we’ve become aware that just as there is an infinity from the cell up to the whole cosmos, there is one in the other direction too, that the subatomic particles and on and on and on and on. So it goes to infinity both ways. But in that chain, each thing is both — each thing that has evolved has both transcended and included the previous thing. And it also becomes something that’s transcended and included by the next thing. So the key concepts are transcend and also include. And the other interesting aspect of that is that at any point in that chain if something goes wrong with a whole on a particular level, then everything that exists above that whole on the chain disappears eventually in time, is doomed, while everything that’s below that whole stays intact. Interesting concept, you know, because it relates to everything. So in music, people have this concept of whether it’s jazz or so-called classical music or pop music or whatever it is, that it has to be new all the time. But the thing that’s key, when I think of somebody like Clare Fischer or Ellington or even Bach, one of the things with Bach, back in Bach’s own time, Bach was not considered to be that important. He was not an innovator. That was not the key thing for him. He was a consolidator. And that was his greatness. Because he was able to understand the ways that different people in different European countries were working with this music that was going on, and get to the point where he actually understood it and could do it better than them or as good as them. In the suites he had to do it in the manner of composition in the manner of dance forms etcetera, you know, that people were using in England. I mean when we listen to it today we don’t hear all that much difference because it’s that Baroque stuff. But if you really get into it, you know I’m not an expert, there are really people who are experts at Baroque music, they could tell you exactly in the English suites what’s the stuff that is unique to the English suites and why that’s typically what they were doing in England at the time, where the French suites the same way, or the Italian concerto. And the same thing with Ellington. The thing that was unique about Ellington’s orchestra was that it was the only big band I think that’s ever existed where every time you heard Ellington’s orchestra you heard the whole history of jazz. Because he didn’t just stop playing pieces that he wrote that were really great pieces in the late 20s and early 30s, but you know, they evolved because new people came in to take over those roles. And in many instances they didn’t even play notes in the solos that were that different from the predecessor. You know, sometimes Lawrence Brown would actually play a Tricky Sam solo. Or sometimes Cootie Williams would play a solo that some earlier plunger player who might have been a better trombone plunger player.
